headline.statement: All four of the paper's significant female-offspring effects in Table 1 -- including the abstract's 81% severe-obesity reduction reported as P < .001 -- have p-values that cannot be recovered from the 95% confidence intervals printed beside them; every one of the four intervals behaves as a 99% interval instead.
headline.evidence: Table 1, female rows, all labelled "ARR (95% CI)": 0.493 (0.292-0.833), P = .002; 0.449 (0.234-0.858), P = .003; 0.396 (0.169-0.931), P = .007; 0.185 (0.046-0.748), P < .001. Read as the labelled 95% intervals, the recovered p-values are 0.0082, 0.0157, 0.0333 and 0.0177 -- 4x to 18x the printed values. The most consequential is the abstract's headline result: a 95% interval of (0.046, 0.748) around 0.185 implies p = 0.018, not p < .001. Each interval reconciles with its printed p only at a 99% level (inferred_confidence_level = 0.99 for all four). Tables 2-4 do not show this signature: the companion maternal headline results 0.613 (0.440-0.855) and 0.217 (0.081-0.582) return inferred_confidence_level = null, i.e. genuine 95% intervals.

findings.title: A "correlation coefficient" of 11.3 is reported for the paper's novel intergenerational analysis
findings.location: Results, "Intergenerational Mobility" (body.md line 303); claim repeated in Discussion
findings.reported: "in the control group, having a mother with severe hypertension was associated with a higher chance (11.3 correlation coefficient) of having a female child with severe hypertension. This association was absent in the treated group, with a significant 0.188 treatment difference in the intergenerational correlation coefficients."
findings.computed: A correlation coefficient is bounded on [-1, 1] by definition, so 11.3 cannot be one. The companion figure in the same sentence -- a 0.188 treatment difference in the SAME intergenerational correlation coefficients -- differs from 11.3 by a factor of about 60, but is entirely coherent with a control-group correlation of 0.113. The overwhelmingly likely cause is a decimal or typesetting slip (0.113 printed as 11.3).
findings.assumptions: Rests on the definitional bound |r| <= 1, which is logically necessary, and on the paper's own word "correlation coefficient". One alternative reading must be named: the Methods describe eTable 8 as showing "estimated regression coefficients", and an unstandardised regression or log-odds coefficient of 11.3 would not violate any bound -- but it could not then be differenced against a companion value of 0.188 on the same scale, so the sentence is incoherent under either reading. The underlying analysis is in eTable 8 of Supplement 2, which was not provided, so the number cannot be diagnosed further.
findings.reproduction: No validated tool in the suite tests a bare reported correlation coefficient for range violation. Verify by reading body.md line 303 against the definition of a correlation coefficient (|r| <= 1).
findings.reproduction_problem: contains placeholder '<' -- not runnable as written; must invoke `metascience`, got 'No'

findings.title: 617 of 618 mothers cannot be 98.8%; no integer count out of 618 yields that percentage
findings.location: Results, paragraph 1 (ethnicity of mothers interviewed at child age 18 y)
findings.reported: "One mother (0.2%) reported Hispanic ethnicity, and 617 mothers (98.8%) reported non-Hispanic ethnicity." Stated denominator n = 618.
findings.computed: GRIM: 98.8% of 618 implies a count of 610.58; the nearest attainable percentages at n = 618 are 98.7% and 98.9%. A GRIM sweep over n = 600-640 returns viable ns of 600-608 and 640 for 98.8% -- 618 is absent. The two exhaustive ethnicity categories also sum to 99.0%, not 100%, off by exactly 1.0 point. The printed count 617/618 = 99.8%, which IS attainable.
findings.assumptions: n = 618 is a stated denominator, not an assumed one: the paper states 618 mothers were interviewed at child age 18 y, the arm split 192 + 426 = 618 reconciles exactly, and the three race counts 5 + 578 + 35 sum to exactly 618. No assumed bound is involved. The benign explanation -- 99.8 mis-set as 98.8 -- is strongly supported, because every other percentage on the same denominator (0.8/93.5/5.7) passes GRIM.

findings.title: Table 1's four significant female effects reconcile with their p-values only as 99% intervals, not the labelled 95%
findings.computed: check_estimate_ci on the log scale recovers p = 0.0082, 0.0157, 0.0333 and 0.0177 respectively against the printed .002, .003, .007 and <.001. All four return inferred_confidence_level = 0.99. Each estimate does sit at its own log-CI midpoint (implied centres 0.4932, 0.4481, 0.3967, 0.1855), so the intervals are internally well formed -- it is the level or the p-values that disagree.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own "95% CI" column heading and its printed p-values. The tool returns 'consistent' per row because it locates an alternative confidence level that reconciles each; the finding is the contradiction with the printed label, which the tool cannot see. A legitimate mechanism exists -- footnotes b and c say the ARR is from logistic regression and the P value tests "the null hypothesis that the treatment effect is 0", so the p may come from the logistic (log-odds) coefficient while the interval is a transformed relative risk. That mechanism is not disclosed and cuts against the pattern being confined to Table 1: the maternal outcomes in Table 4 are far more prevalent (0.5-0.8), where odds ratios and risk ratios diverge most, yet those rows reconcile at 95%.

findings.title: Results described as "significantly less likely" have intervals spanning the null and p-values not below the paper's own threshold
findings.location: Results, "Obesity" paragraph 1, and Table 1 (obesity and severe obesity at age 18 y, Female)
findings.reported: "Nurse-visited female offspring were significantly less likely to have obesity and severe obesity at both ages when considering each time point in isolation and together ... and more than 40% at age 18 years (ARR, 0.561; 95% CI, 0.293-1.075; P = .05)." Table 1 also gives obesity at 18 y, Female: 0.698 (0.455-1.073), P = .08, MHT P = .09. The stated rule is "A 2-sided P < .05 was set as the threshold for significance".
findings.computed: For 0.561 (0.293-1.075): the CI includes the null (upper bound 1.075) and the p recovered from the interval is 0.0813, not .05. For 0.698 (0.455-1.073): the CI includes the null and the recovered p is 0.1004 against a printed .08. Neither age-18 outcome meets the paper's own P < .05 rule, and a printed P of exactly .05 does not satisfy a strict inequality either way.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed intervals, p-values and significance rule. This is a verbal over-claim relative to the numbers in the same table, in the paragraph that introduces the paper's headline result.

findings.title: Printed p-values are not recoverable from the printed intervals across the ARR tables, in both directions
findings.location: Tables 1-4, ARR (95% CI) and P value columns
findings.computed: Recovered p-values 0.4029, 0.0752, 0.0249, 0.0171 and 0.0321 respectively. Across nine checked rows the discrepancy runs in both directions -- recovered p larger for 0.881, 0.784, 0.698, 0.815, 0.605 and 0.663, smaller for 1.454. Nine rows flagged suspicious. Bidirectionality argues against a single systematic transcription error.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the printed table values. This is consistent with the p-values being generated from a different quantity than the intervals (see finding 3) -- a legitimate computation but an internally inconsistent presentation, since a reader cannot recover either quantity from the other. It is not universal: the five difference-scale (LSMD) estimates in the text reconcile cleanly (191.37 g [55.01-327.75], recovered p 0.0060 vs printed .006), as do several text-reported ARRs.

findings.title: The 12-year ethnicity statement cites the 18-year denominator
findings.reported: "Of the mothers interviewed at child age 12 years, 3 (0.5%) self-reported their race as Aleut, Eskimo, or American Indian; 0 as Asian or Pacific Islander; 559 (94.1%) as Black; and 32 (5.4%) as White. All 618 reported non-Hispanic ethnicity."
findings.computed: The three race counts sum to exactly 594, the correct 12-year N (3 + 559 + 32 = 594, difference 0). The ethnicity sentence in the same breath cites 618, which is the 18-year N used correctly in the very next sentence. The 12-year ethnicity denominator is therefore wrong by 24.
findings.assumptions: None; both denominators are stated by the paper (594 mothers interviewed at child age 12 y, 618 at 18 y) and the arm splits 187 + 407 = 594 and 192 + 426 = 618 both reconcile exactly.

findings.title: Identical sex counts are given two different percentage splits in adjacent blocks of Table 1
findings.location: Table 1, "Obesity at age 18 y" vs "Severe obesity at age 18"
findings.reported: Obesity at age 18 y: Overall 605; Female 307 (50.7); Male 297 (49.3). Severe obesity at age 18: Overall 605; Female 307 (50.8); Male 297 (49.2).
findings.computed: The sex counts sum to 604, one short of the stated Overall N of 605 -- which table footnote a explains (lasso-selected control variables with missing values). On denominator 604 the pair (307, 297) gives exactly 50.8/49.2, matching the severe-obesity block. The obesity block's 50.7/49.3 matches no single denominator alongside the printed counts: at n = 605, 50.7% requires k = 307 but 49.3% requires k = 298, not the printed 297; at n = 604, 50.7% requires k = 306.
findings.assumptions: Denominators 604 and 605 are both stated or directly implied by the table. This corrects the Stage-1 statement that no n in 590-620 yields 50.7 with count 307 -- 50.7 alone is attainable at n = 605; what fails is the pair (307, 297) at any single denominator. Substantively minor, but it indicates the No. (%) column was not derived mechanically from one source.

findings.title: A multiplicity-corrected p-value is printed as ".00"
findings.location: Table 4, maternal stage 1 hypertension at age 12 y, Mothers of females
findings.computed: Seven rows across Tables 1, 3 and 4 print a Romano-Wolf corrected p below the uncorrected p. Small reversals are legitimate under a bootstrap stepdown, because the bootstrap null differs from the asymptotic null, so this is not by itself an error and the pattern is deprioritized. What warrants clarification is the single value printed as ".00": read literally it states p = 0, and it is uninformative at that precision. The analogous 12-and-18-year row in the same column prints .002, so the precision convention is inconsistent within one column.
findings.assumptions: The direction-of-inequality expectation is stated from the definition of a familywise stepdown correction, not computed -- no validated tool in the suite reproduces a Romano-Wolf bootstrap correction, so the 69 MHT values could not be recalculated.
findings.reproduction: No validated tool applies. Verify by direct inspection of the two printed p-value columns in Table 4 (body.md line 240) against the definition of a stepdown multiplicity correction.

findings.title: "No effect" is asserted for male offspring and mothers of males on intervals that permit large effects
findings.location: Key Points, Abstract, Results "Obesity" and "Hypertension" paragraphs
findings.reported: "No intervention effect was found for these outcomes among male offspring or mothers of males." "Table 1 shows that NFP had no effect on male offspring obesity." "No differences were significant."
findings.computed: Male offspring obesity at 12 y is ARR 1.454 (0.963-2.197), P = .09: the interval includes the null but remains compatible with a 2.20-fold effect, and is directionally adverse and borderline. Female offspring stage 1 hypertension at 12 and 18 y is 0.539 (0.157-1.852): compatible with a 6.37-fold effect in either direction. Because the paper states no smallest effect size of interest, equivalence cannot be assessed and no conclusion of "no effect" is licensed by these intervals alone.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the printed intervals. The tool correctly declines to judge equivalence in the absence of a stated SESOI, and that refusal is the recorded result. The editorial point is the asymmetry: a P = .05 interval spanning the null is called a significant benefit for females, while a P = .09 interval spanning the null is called no effect for males.

findings.title: Per-arm sample sizes are never reported, which blocks the strongest available check on the proportion columns
findings.location: Tables 1-4, "Proportion, mean (SD)" Control and Treatment columns
findings.reported: Every outcome is a 0/1 indicator reported as a mean and SD by arm (e.g. "0.12 (0.33)" control vs "0.02 (0.16)" treatment), but only a combined row N is given.
findings.computed: DEBIT is the natural check -- for a binary variable the SD is fully determined by the mean and n -- but the verdict flips with the assumed denominator. A first pass using arm sizes inferred from the 228:514 allocation returned three "impossible" rows; every one reverses to consistent at another plausible n (0.31/0.47 impossible at n = 212 but consistent at n = 207 and n = 400; 0.02/0.16 consistent at n = 80 and n = 120; 0.05/0.23 consistent at n = 110). Those three flags were artefacts of assumed denominators and are withdrawn. 19 of 23 rows were consistent at the inferred n.
findings.assumptions: Per rulebook rule 4, no DEBIT verdict on this paper can rise above indeterminate, because every denominator would have to be supplied by the reviewer. A second caveat compounds this: the paper does not state whether these proportions are raw sample means or lasso/IPW-adjusted, and if adjusted the SD is not pinned by the mean at all. There is no evidence of a problem here -- only an inability to test.

not_checked.location: eTable 2 in Supplement 2 -- Balancing Tests, Baseline Covariates
not_checked.reason: The single most significant gap. This is the primary randomization-integrity check and the natural target for csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion (Carlisle/Fujii baseline-similarity analysis). Supplement 2 was not provided, so no baseline p-values or group means/SDs were available and neither tool could be run. The paper asserts only that "The balancing tests showed few baseline differences" -- an unquantified claim that, per rulebook rule 1, is not in itself reassuring. This matters more than usual here because the authors used post-double-selection lasso specifically to correct baseline imbalances, so the extent of those imbalances is load-bearing for every estimate in the paper.

not_checked.location: eTable 3 in Supplement 2 -- Ex-Post Power Calculations
not_checked.reason: verify_power_analysis needs the effect size, alpha, target power and n actually used; the paper states only "at least 80% power (alpha = .05) for the majority of outcomes" without naming the assumed effect size or which outcomes qualify. Separately worth flagging: these are ex-post (post hoc) power calculations computed from observed effects, which are widely regarded as uninformative about a completed study.

Supplement 2 was not provided. This withholds the inverse-probability-weighting robustness analysis (eTable 9), the unbalanced-covariate robustness check (eTable 10), the self-report-exclusion checks (eTables 11-12), the mediation analysis (eTable 7) and the intergenerational correlation analysis (eTable 8) -- the last being the source of the 11.3 correlation coefficient, which therefore cannot be diagnosed further.

The article states "Data Sharing Statement: See Supplement 3" but Supplement 3 was not provided, so whether the underlying data are actually available for reanalysis could not be established either way.

not_checked.location: Figure, quantile regression treatment effects, panels A-F
not_checked.reason: Vector-drawn plots with 90% CI bands and no numeric values in the caption or body. No coefficients, standard errors or deciles are reported anywhere in text, so nothing was digitizable to a checkable statistic; any value read off the marks would be tier-2 figure_pixels provenance and barred from the exact-arithmetic tools in any case.

Reported as bare point estimates with no standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values or component coefficients. Gelbach decomposition inputs are in eTable 7 (unavailable). No validated tool can test a proportion-mediated figure without its variance components.

not_checked.location: Romano-Wolf multiple-hypothesis-testing p-values (69 MHT values across Tables 1-4)
not_checked.reason: No validated tool reproduces a bootstrap stepdown correction. The MHT column was compared against the uncorrected p column by direct inspection only; the corrected values themselves could not be recalculated without the 1000-replication bootstrap and the underlying data.

not_checked.location: Adequacy of the multiplicity blocking structure across the full analysis
not_checked.reason: The Romano-Wolf correction was applied within 6 blocks of 3 outcomes per table -- within-table only, not across the four tables or across the sex strata jointly. No tool in the suite evaluates whether a stated correction's blocking structure is adequate for the full family of tests, so this is recorded for editorial judgment rather than as a tool finding.

not_checked.location: Maternal age at randomization, mean (SD) 18.1 (3.2), n = 742
not_checked.reason: GRIM and GRIMMER were deliberately not run. Age in years is a continuous measure and the paper does not state it was recorded as whole years; applying integer-scale tools to a continuous variable is the most common route to a false accusation. Even if integer-valued, GRIM granularity at n = 742 (1/742 = 0.0013) is far finer than the reported 1 decimal place, so the test would be vacuous.

not_checked.location: Cell counts underlying every ARR in Tables 1-4
not_checked.reason: Only combined row Ns are given, never per-arm sizes or event counts, so recalc_independent_t, recalc_chi_squared and reconstruct_2x2 could not be applied to any outcome. Verification had to proceed entirely from estimate/CI/p triples, which are one level less primitive than the rulebook's preferred starting point (rule 10).

limitations: This agent reads text and does not see figures. The Figure (quantile regression panels A-F) was not read; its 90% CI bands and coefficients were not assessed, and the claim that they 'confirmed' the main results could not be checked.

Only the main article body was available. Supplements 1, 2 and 3 -- containing the CONSORT table, the baseline balance table, the analytic plan, the power calculations, all robustness checks, the mediation and intergenerational analyses, and the data sharing statement -- were not provided. Several findings, and the largest coverage gap, follow directly from that.

The paper reports no APA-style NHST statistics (no t(df), F(df1,df2), r or chi-squared with df), so statcheck returned zero results and the entire p-value verification burden fell on reconciling estimates against their confidence intervals.

Confidence-interval reconciliation uses a normal approximation on the log scale. Where a paper computes intervals by another method (profile likelihood, bootstrap, robust or cluster-adjusted standard errors), small discrepancies can arise legitimately; the discrepancies reported here are larger than that mechanism comfortably explains, but the possibility is not excluded.
The coverage counts below are an accounting estimate, not an exact tally; the tables and locations listed are exact.

tables_checked: Table 1 (offspring obesity and severe obesity by sex, 18 ARR rows)
Table 2 (maternal obesity and severe obesity by offspring sex, 18 ARR rows)
Table 3 (offspring stage 1 and 2 hypertension by sex, 15 ARR rows)
Table 4 (maternal stage 1 and 2 hypertension by offspring sex, 18 ARR rows)
Results paragraph 1 race/ethnicity counts, percentages and denominators
Methods participant accounting and arm splits

report_markdown:
## What the paper claims

This is the 18-year follow-up of the Memphis Nurse-Family Partnership trial, in which 742 low-income pregnant women were randomized to nurse home visiting (228) or to transportation plus developmental screening alone (514). The authors report that nurse-visited female offspring had substantially lower rates of obesity and severe obesity at ages 12 and 18 years, and that nurse-visited mothers of female offspring had lower rates of stage 1 and stage 2 hypertension, with no corresponding effects among males or mothers of males. The authors are explicit that obesity, hypertension and sex-moderation were not primary or secondary outcomes in the original protocol -- these are exploratory analyses of an existing trial, and the paper says so in its first limitation. That candour is worth crediting up front, and it frames everything below.

## What the checks found, and what they did not

The trial's participant accounting is sound. Every randomization and follow-up split reconciles exactly (228 + 514 = 742; 187 + 407 = 594; 192 + 426 = 618; 180 + 398 = 578; 194 + 435 = 629), the sample sizes carry the irregular signature of real 18-year attrition rather than roundness, and the sex-stratified counts that fall 1-2 short of their row totals are adequately explained by the table footnote about lasso-selected controls with missing values. Cross-table duplication detection over 55 proportion cells found no improbable overlap between independent sources. The difference-scale (LSMD) estimates in the text reconcile cleanly with their intervals and p-values. These are not trivial passes, and they argue against a general failure of care.

The effect sizes also survive a plausibility check that they superficially fail. An 81% relative risk reduction in severe obesity sounds extraordinary, but on the standardised scale the female severe-obesity contrast (0.12 vs 0.02) is Hedges' g = 0.35, sitting at the medicine_rct field median of 0.30. A large relative reduction on a rare binary outcome is a modest absolute and standardised effect. This should not be flagged as too-good-to-be-true, and I want to say so plainly rather than let silence imply otherwise.

What does not hold up is the correspondence between the estimates, the intervals and the p-values in the ARR tables -- and the correspondence between those numbers and the sentences written about them.

## Why the interval problem matters most

The four significant female-offspring rows in Table 1 are the paper's offspring story. Each is labelled a 95% CI, and each reconciles with its printed p-value only if it is in fact a 99% interval. The abstract's headline -- ARR 0.185, 95% CI 0.046-0.748, P < .001 -- implies p = 0.018 if the interval is what the column heading says it is. That is a factor of roughly eighteen, and it lands on the number a reader is most likely to carry away.

There is a legitimate mechanism available: footnotes b and c say the ARR comes from logistic regression and the P value tests the null that "the treatment effect is 0", so the p may be a Wald test on the log-odds coefficient while the interval is a transformed relative risk. If so, the two quantities simply are not recoverable from one another, and the presentation should say so. But that explanation predicts the mismatch should be worst where odds ratios and risk ratios diverge most -- the common maternal outcomes in Table 4, with prevalences of 0.5 to 0.8. Those are precisely the rows that reconcile at 95%. The pattern is localised to Table 1 rather than systematic, and across the wider tables the discrepancies run in both directions. I cannot reconcile that with any single mechanical cause, and it is the first thing I would put to the authors.

Adjacent to this is a verbal problem that needs no statistics to see. The sentence introducing the headline result claims female offspring were "significantly less likely to have obesity and severe obesity at both ages when considering each time point in isolation and together". At age 18 in isolation, obesity is ARR 0.698 (0.455-1.073), P = .08 and severe obesity is ARR 0.561 (0.293-1.075), P = .05. Both intervals include no effect; neither p falls below the paper's own stated rule of "a 2-sided P < .05". Meanwhile a male-offspring result with a wider interval on the same side of the threshold -- ARR 1.454 (0.963-2.197), P = .09, directionally adverse -- is reported as "no effect on male offspring obesity". The same evidential standard is not being applied to the positive female findings and the null male findings, and since the sex contrast is the paper's central novelty, that asymmetry does real work.

## Multiplicity and verifiability

The Romano-Wolf correction is applied within six blocks of three outcomes per table. That is within-table only: it does not span the four tables, nor the sex strata jointly, and the main tables alone contain 69 ARR tests of outcomes the authors state were not prespecified. "Controls the familywise error rate" is accurate for each block and considerably weaker than it sounds for the analysis as a whole. The supporting power claim is an ex-post calculation, which is uninformative about a completed study.

Two omissions limit what anyone can check. Per-arm sample sizes appear nowhere, only combined row Ns, which defeats DEBIT on the binary proportion columns and blocks every count-based recalculation -- verification had to run entirely on estimate/CI/p triples, one level less primitive than one would want. And the balance table (eTable 2) was not available. That gap is load-bearing rather than incidental: the authors used post-double-selection lasso expressly "to correct estimates for baseline imbalances", so the size of those imbalances conditions every estimate in the paper, and the only statement about them is the unquantified "showed few baseline differences". No baseline-similarity or dispersion test could be run, and I want to be clear that this is an untested question, not a passed one.

## Verdict

The two impossibilities -- a correlation coefficient of 11.3 and 617 of 618 given as 98.8% -- both have obvious benign readings (0.113 and 99.8%) and neither, on its own, would change a conclusion. Taken with the interval and significance problems, however, they describe a manuscript whose numbers were not checked against each other before publication. The trial infrastructure looks real and the participant accounting is clean; it is the inferential layer that does not hold together. The headline offspring findings, as printed, are not supported by the intervals printed beside them, and the claims of significance at age 18 are contradicted by the paper's own significance rule. I would not rely on the reported precision of these results without a correction from the authors clarifying the confidence level and the origin of the p-values in Table 1, and without sight of the baseline balance table and per-arm counts.
